← Priority Guide
Getting Unblocked
Being blocked on someone else’s feedback, or waiting for a response to a question is a normal and expected part of reviewing. It doesn’t mean something has gone wrong. When you are blocked, don’t just wait for a reply. Send a single, clear question that, if answered, would unblock you immediately. Here are some thinking prompts to help you create your one, clear question:

What knowledge am I missing, and why does it matter? Name the one decision you need made or piece of information you’re missing. The “why does it matter” part of this question is especially important because it determines whether the question is leading you off track (see 6. Staying on Track). Good answers to this question sound like this:

“I need to know if this frame in this figma is supposed to be clickable, because that changes the role I’d recommend for annotations”
“I don’t know if this is an AT bug or general bug, and that impacts how I file it.”
“I don’t know enough about aria-describedby vs. aria-description to know which to recommend here, but I can tell this information should be exposed in a description.”


Who (or what) has the authority to answer my question? Use static resources (resources that aren’t people) before asking a coworker. This makes your knowledge base stronger and helps you learn.

For a technical question like the aria-description one above, you might read MDN, Deque resources, or the aria spec.
For questions on a particular figma file, you might read the PRD for the feature or look through figma comments.
For bug filing or testing questions, often the answer lies in hands-on verification. See the Bug Verification & Filing docs for more info.
Some questions have to be answered by people, that’s okay :)


What have I already tried? What did I learn from trying? If you’ve checked some resources or tested some options, write them out. For each resource, think about what you found or didn’t find. Do your findings change where you should look next? Did you get partial information which changes the knowledge you’re after? For example:

“I looked in the core tree to see if the node was present. I did see it there, which tells me this isn’t a generic bug. I guess that leaves platform bug or AT bug, so I should check the flowchart for what to do next.”
“I read through the figma file but I don’t see any comments about this particular control, so I’ll @ the designer to see if they intend it to be clickable or static.”
“I learned from Deque that aria-description takes a string and aria-describedby takes an id, but the text I want to reference is in a shadow root, so I don’t think I can link to its id directly. I need to ask if there’s a technical workaround, or if aria-description with duplicated text is the preferred solution.”



Consider these prompts as you draft your question, but do not include all the information in your message. See section 4, “When you need help, lead with your question” for more information on formatting your request.
After you’ve posted your question, use the flowchart to make decisions about what to do while you wait to be unblocked.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/priority-guid.title: 4. Non-Review Work
Work/Documentation/Reviews/priority-guid.content:
← Priority Guide
Non-Review Work
The “Extras”
In addition to review work, your job consists of other tasks with blurrier deadlines. Here are some of them:



































ItemTaskDeadlineYou have a meeting with your managerYou need to pre-fill meeting notes and collect your thoughts for the discussionBefore the meeting startsYou have need-infos on BugzillaYou need to read, understand, and respond to these questions< 3 daysYou have mentions on slackYou need to read, understand, and respond to these mentions< 1 dayYou have to complete your performance reviewYou need to collect information about your work and complete a writeupDeadline usually shared 1-2 weeks in advanceYou need to be reimbursed for internet expensesYou need to receive your internet bill, create a report on Expensify and submit it for the month< 6 months after expense is incurred
When an “extra” task is at or approaching its deadline, you should act on it. It might supersede review work temporarily. This is expected. Check with your manager or mentor for more guidance on fitting “extras” into your schedule.

Self Check: Try to plan out your week in advance to fit in items with flexible deadlines (e.g. need-infos or performance review work) ahead of their due date. You might anticipate recurring “extras” (like responding to need-infos) with a static block of time on your calendar, ex. 20 minutes after lunch every Tuesday. If the time comes and there’s no work to do, great! But if there is work, you know you’ve got time to do it.

Optional Tasks
Some tasks may seem required, but are in fact optional. You should not do these if doing so would prevent you from meeting a deadline on a review or an item in the “extras” list above. Optional tasks include things like:

The biweekly MoCo meeting
Lightning talks or demos
Reading threads you are not directly tagged in (including in the accessibility channel)
MoFo-related activities/meetings

Taking Breaks
It is not expected you work 9a-5p without breaks :) In fact, you should be taking at least 30m for lunch and at least two other 10m breaks throughout the work day. Micro breaks to stand up, stretch, get a snack, make some coffee, etc. are also important.
Breaks aren’t time lost — they protect your work. Pushing hour after hour without stepping away leads to burnout, and tired work is slower and less accurate. This impacts quality. Even your busiest day should include at least the three breaks above.
The harder part is knowing when to break.

Don’t break at the first sign of difficulty. When something is confusing or hard, that is usually the moment right before it clicks. Stepping away then loses your progress and forces you to work even harder to recall it when you come back. The first feeling of confusion is a cue to stay with it a little longer, not to stop.
Don’t push for hours. If you’ve been heads-down for ~60–90 minutes, or stuck on the same problem with no progress, that is a stopping point — take the break even if you’d rather keep going.

When difficulty hits, take one step towards a solution before stepping away: re-read the spec, test one more platform/AT. Then, write down exactly what’s confusing, what you’ve tried, and what might be next. This gives you a plan to come back to after the break. See 3. Getting Unblocked for more.
Even when you’re not blocked, you should make time for breaks. Here are some good points to take a break, even if there’s more you could do right now on the current task:

You’ve been focused for ~60–90 minutes
You finished a discrete piece (ex. a figma section, a filed bug, a sent message) and have deadlines approaching for “extra” work
You’re genuinely blocked and followed the steps in 3. Getting Unblocked


Self-check: Try setting a timer for 60 minutes when you start a new piece of work. When the timer goes off, if you’re at a good stopping point, take a break. If you’re in the middle of something when it rings, identify your next stopping point. Take a break after you’re done.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/priority-guid.title: 5. You're Doing it Right
Work/Documentation/Reviews/priority-guid.content:
← Priority Guide
You’re Doing it Right!
Even with the flowchart, you might find yourself ruminating or worrying about working on the “right thing”. Working on the right thing will not always feel calm, easy, or stress-free. Here are some things to remember:


If you are working the highest-ranked item you can make progress on, you are doing the right thing. Full stop. That is the definition. This does not mean you will be “caught up.”


Feeling rushed is not the same as being behind. Your deadlines are the handoff dates in the sheet. If you are working on a high-priority item before its handoff date, and you are progressing, you are on track. This is true even if the queue looks long. A long queue is the team’s backlog, not a measure of you.


You don’t have to catch everything. Quality means that what you do report is accurate, clear, and complete the first time — not that you found every possible issue. (More on this in writing-findings-and-recommendations.)


When you suspect priorities may have shifted due to an anomaly, ask for clarification with a plan attached. Use this frame:

“I’m planning to work on [X] next, because [reason]. Does [situation] change the priority, or should I stick with my plan?”



Here’s an example: “I’m planning to work on Firefox Referrals next, because it is the highest priority item in the queue. Does yesterday’s discussion in moco about focusing on mobile mean I should work on the Mobile Containers review first, or should I stick with my plan?”

Work/Documentation/Reviews/priority-guid.title: 6. Staying on Track
Work/Documentation/Reviews/priority-guid.content:
← Priority Guide
Staying on Track
As you work, you may find yourself off-track or starting to move off-track/into the weeds. None of these situations are a problem if you catch them. Here’s how to move forward after you realise you’re moving off track.

































SignalCorrectionAsking a designer or engineer when they will respond to your feedback or question, after the feedback/question has been posted.Asking the question or providing the feedback is enough. You do NOT need to follow up again. Work on the highest-ranked review.Working on follow-up while a higher-ranked first-pass review is actionableSwitch to the first-pass review, use the flowchart.Several reviews half-done, but not finishedPick the highest-ranked one and take it as far as it goes before touching another.Deep in a single token/spec/edge case for a long timeFormulate a question about your core confusion, ask it, move on to something else while you wait for a reply.Polishing artifacts (screenshots, GIFs, write-ups) beyond what’s neededStop at “clear enough to act on.”Trying to learn about a property (ex. aria-describedby) because it came up in a review, even though it isn’t knowledge you need to make the recommendation right now.Park it as a separate note/bug on your list of “extra” tasks; return to the recommendation at hand and complete it.

Review Workflow — Walkthrough
This walks through the review workflow one decision at a time, the companion to review-workflow-flowchart. It covers how to move a review from pickup to close — when to start, when to stop, and what order to work in. For the detailed accessibility checks you perform during a review, see Accessibility Review Process.
Like the bug-verification process, this is a decision tree, not a checklist. Each step tells you whether the next step is needed. You will often stop early — that is the design working, not you cutting corners.
Contents

1. Before you pick up the review
2. Check the handoff date
3. If the handoff date has passed
4. Confirm the scope
5. Confirm the priority
6. Run the review
7. Close the review
8. Flow Diagram

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 1. Before you pick up the review
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
Before you pick up the review
Every review starts the same way, whether it is brand new or one you are resuming after a break:

Open the review tracker and find the row.
Note the priority (the ranking in the sheet) and the handoff date.
Start your time tracking.


Self-check: Before you open Figma or a build, answer two questions: Is this still worth doing? (handoff date) and Is this the right thing to be doing right now? (priority). The rest of this page is how to answer them.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 2. Check the handoff date
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
Check the handoff date
The handoff date is the definitive deadline for a design review — “pencils down.” After it, engineering has started and your feedback may not be incorporated. Check it every time you pick up or resume a review, not just the first time.

Handoff date is in the future → the review is live. Continue to 4. Confirm the scope.
Handoff date has passed, or is blank → do not start reviewing yet. Go to 3. If the handoff date has passed.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.filePath: Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workflow-walkthrough/3. If the handoff date has passed.md
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 3. If the handoff date has passed
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
If the handoff date has passed
A passed date doesn’t automatically mean the review is dead — it means you need one piece of information before spending time: has engineering started or finished?
Step 1 — Ask the designer first. Post in the review’s accessibility-channel thread (not a DM):

Hi [name], I noticed the review for [REVIEW NAME] has a handoff date of [DATE], which has already passed. Before I dig in — has engineering already started, or finished, this work?

Step 2 — If the designer doesn’t know, ask the PM, or the engineering lead.

Reaching out to a PM directly is fine.
Reaching out to an engineering manager goes through Frank first — loop him in rather than contacting them yourself.

Step 3 — Act on the answer:





















AnswerWhat to doEngineering has finishedDrop the review. The feedback can’t land. Note it in the tracker and move on.Engineering hasn’t started or is ongoingAsk for a new handoff date (“When will engineering work on this until?”), update the sheet, and continue to 4. Confirm the scope.No timeline availableLeave it out of your active queue until there is one. A review with no live deadline isn’t worth working yet.

Self-check: You are not deciding whether the work matters — you are confirming whether your feedback can still be used. If it can’t, dropping it is the correct call, not a failure.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 4. Confirm the scope
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
Confirm the scope
Review what is new or changed, not the whole surface.

Identify which parts of the UI are new or updated. Exclude business-as-usual / unchanged UI.
If the scope is unclear, confirm with the designer in the thread before reviewing — don’t guess. (This is a quick question, not a research task.)
Content added after the initial review was submitted is follow-up work, not part of this first pass. It doesn’t need a brand-new review request from the designer; you can track it as follow-up. (See 5. Confirm the priority for how follow-up is ranked.)
If a reusable component is used unchanged, its annotations/HCM are waived — ask for a link to the component library instead. Checking whether something is reusable is a quick step, not something that should double your review time.


Self-check: Can you state, in one sentence, what you are reviewing and what you are deliberately not reviewing? If not, ask the designer before continuing.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 5. Confirm the priority
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
Confirm the priority
Two simple rules settle almost every “what should I do first?” question. (The full version, including what to do when you’re blocked or your queue is empty, is in priority-guide.)

First-pass reviews outrank follow-up work — always, regardless of how “important” the follow-up’s project is.
Order comes from the ranking in the sheet, not from whichever deadline is soonest. Work the highest-ranked item you can make progress on. Deadlines decide whether to do a review; the ranking decides what order.


Self-check: If you’re about to work on follow-up while a higher-ranked first-pass review is actionable, pause — the first-pass review comes first.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 6. Run the review
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
Run the review
Now do the actual accessibility review. The complete reference for what to check — annotations, focus order, contrast, HCM, controls, states, content, and the rest — lives in Accessibility Review Process. A few workflow habits that make the review go smoothly:

Guess and check. Before each section, finish the sentence “I’d expect to see ___,” then verify what the design actually shows. This is faster and catches more than reviewing cold.
Keep a running list of open questions as you go; resolve them at the end rather than stopping the flow each time.
When you hit a real bug, file it using bug-verification-and-filing-revised — that decides generic vs platform/AT-specific and how to scope it.
Time-box rabbit holes. If you’re deep in “which exact token / which exact value” for a long time, note the question and move on rather than getting stuck. Getting an answer later is cheaper than stalling the review.


Self-check: When you write a finding, are you stating a clear recommendation the team can act on — not just listing options? See writing-findings-and-recommendations.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.title: 7. Close the review
Work/Documentation/Reviews/review-workfl.content:
← Review Workflow — Walkthrough
Close the review
Before you mark it complete:

Resolve or note any remaining open questions.
Notify the requester in the accessibility-channel thread (tag them) that the review is complete.
Update the tracker status.
Flag any S2s explicitly — they are ship blockers, so the team needs to know about them with urgency.
Note any follow-up: who still needs contacting, what questions remain, and whether the review surfaced a new team or design-system standard worth sharing.


Self-check: Have you said, clearly and in one place, “this review is complete, here are the findings, here are the S2s”? That sentence is the deliverable.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
This is a reviewer’s guide to HCM. It builds the mental model you need to review HCM mockups and catch HCM bugs — so you can reason about whether something is right, instead of searching for a file that tells you the answer. It stands on its own; you don’t need the engineering HCM docs to use it.
It complements the HCM section of Accessibility Review Process (the checklist) by explaining the why behind it. For writing up what you find, see writing-findings-and-recommendations.
Contents

1. HCM Quick Reference
2. What is High Contrast Mode
3. Style by Function
4. Visual Distinctions Matter
5. Using Tokens
6. You can reason this out

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.title: 1. HCM Quick Reference
Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
← Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
HCM Quick Reference
For each element in the mockup (or each control as you review a build with Windows HCM / Night Sky on) ask yourself:

What is this type of control? (button / link / text / input / disabled / selected) → which system colour pair should it resolve to?
Does the token used match that? If it uses a custom token, does it resolve to the right system colour?
Are all states represented correctly — default, hover, active, focus, selected, disabled, error?
Does form survive? Any visual distinction that exists in the default theme should still be visible in HCM (border replaces shadows, etc.).
Anything unspecified? New token with no HCM mapping → flag to design systems with usage context.


The one-sentence version: In HCM, name what each element is, use the system colour that means that, make sure no distinction or shape gets lost — and don’t worry about contrast ratios, they don’t apply here.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.title: 2. What is High Contrast Mode
Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
← Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
What is High Contrast Mode?
In High Contrast Mode, the operating system throws away the design’s colours and repaints everything from a tiny palette of system colours. The important part: each system colour has a meaning — “this is body text,” “this is a button,” “this is disabled,” “this is a link,” “this is selected.”
The design’s only job in HCM is to tell the OS what each element is, by using the system colour that matches its purpose.
Two consequences follow:

You do not check contrast ratios in HCM. If the correct system colours are used for the correct purposes, the OS guarantees they’re readable. A contrast bug never “carries over” into HCM from light/dark mode — HCM is a different system entirely.
The design system should adapt automatically. Your review question for any element is: “What does this resolve to under forced-colors — and does that match what the element is semantically?” Or, even simpler: “If the developer did nothing special, would this come out right?”


Self-check: If you’re about to report a “contrast problem” in HCM, stop. Re-ask the real HCM question: is the right system colour being used for what this element is?

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.title: 3. Style by Function
Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
← Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
Style by Function
Elements that look unusual or custom in the default theme still require a system colour pair based on what they functionally are:

A ghost / borderless / icon button looks transparent or chrome-less — but it’s still a button, so in HCM it takes ButtonFace / ButtonText (plus a border so its shape survives). It does not stay transparent.
A control that’s styled like a button but navigates somewhere is functionally a link → LinkText + underline. A control styled like a link but performs an action is a button → button colours. Match the colour to the behaviour.
A divider, a decorative icon → CanvasText (non-interactive)

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.title: 4. Visual Distinctions Matter
Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
← Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
Visual Distinctions Matter
HCM has far fewer colours, so things that were distinguished by gradients, shadows, etc. in the default theme can disappear in HCM. Two rules protect against that:

No loss of form. If two things look different in the default theme — a selected vs unselected row, a hovered vs default state, a card vs its background — they must still look different in HCM. If a system colour change won’t carry the distinction, the design needs a border or another non-colour form difference. Watch for distinctions that silently disappear in the HCM mockup.
A “contrasting border” is a shape requirement, not a contrast ratio. Because backgrounds like ButtonFace and Canvas can look similar in some HCM themes, a control can lose its edges and blend into the page. A border keeps its shape readable. When an HCM spec calls for a contrasting border, it means “make sure the control’s outline is still visible” — it is not asking you to compute a ratio.
Shadows don’t exist in HCM. box-shadow and text-shadow compute to none under forced-colors. If something relied on a shadow to separate it from the background (a popup, a card, a drag preview), it needs a border instead in HCM.


Self-check: When transitioning to HCM, does any visible distinction vanish? If yes, the item needs a border or form difference.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.title: 5. Using Tokens
Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
← Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
Using Tokens
Tokens can come from many sources. Here are some common origins:

The HCM Figma library is the defaul tsource of truth. When making a new HCM spec, start with it and its tokens.
Experimental libraries are not authoritative for HCM. Nova, “Desktop Components (Experimental),” and similar are works in progress — in many cases their HCM mapping hasn’t been done yet (some HCM tokens don’t exist at all and are temporarily standing in with button tokens).
Custom tokens are fine — as long as they resolve to the correct system colour under forced-colors. A component using its own custom token does not have to be swapped to “Desktop styles.” The only question is whether that token comes out as the right system colour.

When evaluating a token
Don’t assume a mapping exists. Instead:

















SituationWhat to doExisting token from design systems libraryVerify the token has the expected HCM value, then use it. If it is wrong, flag it to design systems on slack.New token, no HCM spec yetFlag it to design systems on slack with usage context — what it’s used on (button fill? text? border?) — so the correct system colour can be decided.

Self-check: If your answer depends on “what does this experimental library show,” stop — that’s not the source of truth. Either the element’s function tells you the colour, or the token is unspecified and needs flagging.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.title: 6. You can reason this out
Work/Documentation/Reviews/reviewing-hig.content:
← Reviewing High Contrast Mode (HCM)
You can reason this out!
You don’t need an authoritative Figma file to know the answer. If you know what an element is, you know what system colour it should resolve to — and that reasoning is yours to make and to state plainly. Reach for the HCM library to confirm your answer, not to give yourself permission to have one.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.title: 0. index
Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.content:
Writing Findings & Recommendations
In review work, your reasoning is the deliverable. When a designer or engineer comes to the accessibility team, they don’t want a list of everything that’s true about ARIA — they want to know what to do, stated clearly, so they can act without coming back to ask for more info. This page describes how to write emphatic, stand-alone accessibility advice.
It pairs with bug-verification-and-filing-revised (the mechanics of bug reports) and Accessibility Review Process (what to look for when doing a review).
Contents

1. Give a single, strong recommendation
2. Be emphatic — own your conclusion
3. Why asks for your reasoning, not a citation
4. When you need help, lead with your question
5. Match the feedback to the audience
6. Ensure quality by double-checking, not double-testing

Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.title: 1. Give a single, strong recommendation
Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.content:
← Writing Findings & Recommendations
1. Give a single, strong recommendation
The most common way a finding misses is by presenting several options and leaving the reader to choose. The reader usually can’t choose — they’re asking for your expertise.

❌ “Form validation can be conveyed several ways. ARIA offers aria-invalid, aria-describedby, aria-errormessage, and live regions; HTML offers the required attribute. There are trade-offs between them, which I need to learn more about, but I think [X] is different from [Y]. You’ll want to pick the one that works for you.”
✅ “Use aria-invalid on the field plus aria-errormessage pointing to the error ID. Don’t use an alert. Here’s why: [one line]. Here’s the exact frame in figma where I’d apply this annotation [link].”

State the conclusion first. Give the reasoning second. Do not offer information the team isn’t asking for, or information that they don’t need right now. There may be several ways to accomplish their goal, but only the recommended route is relevant when giving feedback.

Self-check: Could the reader implement your finding from the first two sentences alone? If they’d have to ask “so which one should I do? do I do all of these?”, revise.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.title: 2. Be emphatic — own your conclusion
Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.content:
← Writing Findings & Recommendations
2. Be emphatic — own your conclusion
“Emphatic” here means clear and authoritative. You did the analysis, now you need to say what you found and mean it. Hedging (phrases like: “maybe,” “I might be overthinking this,” “sorry if this is wrong”) buries a correct answer and makes the reader unsure whether to act on your recommendation.
Use these frames:

























SituationFrameStraightforward recommendation”I recommend X because Y.”Requirement-backed”X is a violation of [WCAG SC #]. The fix is Z.”You changed your mind”I initially suggested A. Having learned B, I now recommend C because D.”Holding a line under pushback”Thanks for the update — the contrast is much improved. It’s still below the 3:1 WCAG requirement, and automated tools will flag it, so we do need to meet it.”
Here’s how you can rework this in practise:

❌ “I think the tab order should probably follow reading order? I might be wrong but that’s my guess.”
✅ “Keep the tab order matching the visual reading order (left-to-right). There’s no requirement to focus primary before secondary buttons — WCAG 2.4.3 only asks that focus order preserve meaning, which reading order already does.”


Self-check: Read your conclusion back. Is there a hedge (phrases like: “maybe,” “I might be overthinking this,” “sorry if this is wrong”) you can delete without losing meaning? Delete it to make your position stronger.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.title: 3. Why asks for your reasoning, not a citation
Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.content:
← Writing Findings & Recommendations
3. “Why?” asks for your reasoning, not a citation
When someone asks why you recommended something, they are asking for your rationale — the principle behind it — not for an external document that “proves” your recommendation is right. A standard (WCAG, the APG, a spec) backs up your judgment; it doesn’t replace it.

❌ Do not: Spend time hunting for a prior note/ticket that justifies your answer or shows where Morgan or Anna made the same choice before replying.
✅ Do justify from principles: “Text inputs use SelectedItem for the focus outline because entering an input creates a text-selection/editing state, whereas a button just receives focus — so they’re semantically different. [Cite the standard with a link, if one applies.]”

If you can explain why from principles, you’re done. Reach for a citation to strengthen the point, not to grant yourself permission.

Self-check: Can you answer “why?” in your own words right now, without opening another document? If yes, write that. If no, identify the gap in your own knowledge. After you resolve it, come back and write the “why?” answer in your own words, from scratch.

Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.content:
← Writing Findings & Recommendations
4. When you need help, lead with your question
When giving feedback, you might come across a grey area or a gap in your knowledge. In these moments, you’ll have to consult other members of the team for help.
Background research, or the context for “Why am I asking?” is important, but it shouldn’t obscure your question. Put a single, specific question first in your message; offer context after for anyone who wants it.

❌ [a few paragraphs of investigation] “and I’m wondering… thoughts?”
✅ “Is the cursor-pointer issue on the toggle worth filing as a separate S3? My instinct is to keep it as part of the main issue, because we did that for Bug X (Background below 🧵)”

If you have several questions, number them and make each answerable on its own. When threading messages on slack, always put the question in the top level thread. Do not start threads with just the topic, ex. “Drag and drop question 🧵” or “Follow-up for bug ”

Self-check: Is there exactly one clear question (or ask) the reader can answer in one reply? If a reader read only your first line, would they know what you need?

Work/Documentation/Reviews/writing-findi.content:
← Writing Findings & Recommendations
5. Match the feedback to the audience
The same finding is written differently depending on who acts on it:

Designers act in Figma → Your feedback should reference their actual frames, use component/token/library names, and say what to change in the mock. Avoid describing complex ARIA patterns or referencing AT quirks. Simple ARIA values are okay, like “This needs aria-haspopup=menu in the annotation notes.”
Engineers act in code → Your feedback should give the role/name/state specifics, the attribute, and where it goes. Complex technical discussion is okay, but it should still be easy to follow. Frontend engineers do not have the same background as accessibility engineers, make sure you explain and define domain specific terms when talking to engineers outside of the a11y team.

In all cases, give the team the quick version of feedback they can act on, and hold off on sharing the deeper reasoning until/if they ask for it.

6. Ensure quality by double-checking, not double-testing
Quality is not “I tested everything.” Quality is “everything I reported is accurate, concise, and complete the first time.” A finding that’s caught but reported inaccurately creates a second round of work, which costs more than the issue itself.
Before you send a finding or file a bug, spend a few minutes double-checking the conclusion. Note: this doesn’t mean re-testing or testing more. Read your writing and ask:

Have I stated the problem, specifically — not “this isn’t accessible,” or “that won’t work” but what is absent or incorrect?
Did I strip out the justification/working-out-my-thinking that the reader doesn’t need?
Did I lead with my recommendation, providing one clear option for my audience?

(The bug-specific version of this lives in bug-verification-and-filing-revised.)
